birds.note: The coastal 'fannini' subspecies stays year-round; Stanley Park has a big rookery.
Thousands gather on the Harrison and Squamish rivers for the winter salmon runs.
The chickadee of the wet coastal forests, with a rich chestnut back.
Nests on pilings and channel markers all along the coast and lakes.
Waddles among sunbathers at Boulders Beach near Cape Town.
The world's largest bird; the Little Karoo was the hub of the feather boom.
Named for its loud 'ha-ha-hadeda' call, the country's unofficial alarm clock.
Found only in the fynbos of the Western Cape, sipping from proteas and ericas.
Pink from the carotenoids in the shrimp it sweeps up with its spoon-shaped bill.
The 'snake bird' swims with only its neck above water, then dries its wings in the sun.
Lives almost entirely on apple snails; its wailing scream is a classic Everglades night sound.
Probes the mud with its curved red bill; the most numerous wading bird in South Florida.
A giant kingfisher whose dawn chorus sounds like raucous laughter.
The pink-and-grey cockatoo; 'galah' is also Aussie slang for a fool.
Brush-tipped tongue for lapping nectar; noisy flocks fill suburban trees.
A tall crane famous for its leaping, bowing courtship dance.
Males trail emerald tail streamers up to two feet long through cloud forest.
Its huge, rainbow-coloured bill is mostly hollow and surprisingly light.
Swings its racket-tipped tail like a pendulum when it spots a predator.
Sits still for long spells, then sallies out to snatch fruit or insects.
Males show off their bright blue feet in a high-stepping courtship dance.
More than a dozen species, each with a bill shaped for its island's food.
The only penguin that lives on the equator.
Nearly the whole world population breeds on Española island.
Voted the UK's national bird in 2015 and a regular on Christmas cards.
Can carry a dozen sand eels crosswise in its bill at once.
Sings non-stop while hovering so high it can vanish from sight.
Tiny, but with one of the loudest songs for its size of any British bird.
India's national bird; the peacock's train has around 200 display feathers.
The female seals herself into a tree hole to nest while the male feeds her.
One of the commonest garden birds from the Himalayan foothills to the south.
A bold, chattering city bird found in almost every Indian town.
Rift Valley soda lakes like Nakuru and Bogoria can turn pink with them.
The largest living bird; Kenya also has the blue-legged Somali Ostrich.
A safari favourite named for its tumbling, rolling display flight.
Builds enormous domed nests that can hold a person's weight.
Flightless and nocturnal, with nostrils at the very tip of its long bill.
The world's heaviest parrot, flightless and nocturnal, with only a few hundred left.
Thought extinct for 50 years until it was rediscovered in Fiordland in 1948.
A purple swamphen that flicks its white undertail as it strides through paddocks.
Alaska's state bird turns pure white in winter.
Winters in openings in the Bering Sea ice.
The largest loon, breeding on Arctic tundra lakes.
Grows golden head plumes for the breeding season.
Raises its crest like a fan; its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call gives it its name.
One of the heaviest flying birds; Spain holds most of the world's population.
Huge colonies soar over the gorges of Monfragüe.
Nests on church towers and pylons all across Extremadura.
